query: In high-entropy alloys, what governs superconducting behavior and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, identify a controlled comparison against a baseline that could reveal the governing cause, predict the relative observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, define its boundary conditions, state what prior evidence would make it plausible, and specify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In phonon‐mediated high-entropy alloy superconductors, the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) is primarily controlled by the average valence electron count (VEC) that tunes the electronic density of states and electron–phonon coupling strength, rather than by the level of atomic disorder.
generation.material_initial_state: A body-centered cubic high-entropy alloy with random atomic distribution, for example, a [TaNb]0.31(TiZrHf)0.69-type alloy known to be a phonon mediated s-wave superconductor in the dirty limit.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the alloy composition by substituting one constituent element (e.g., replacing Zr with uranium or another element with a different valence electron contribution) to modify the average VEC while keeping the overall degree of structural disorder and the BCC structure essentially unchanged.
generation.conditions: Experiments should be performed on alloys that are in the phonon-mediated, weak-coupling BCS s-wave superconducting regime, under ambient pressure and at low temperatures (Tc below ~10 K), ensuring similar levels of disorder (dirty limit) across samples.
generation.structural_mediator: The random, multi-element BCC crystalline framework ensures that while atomic disorder is inherent, it remains consistent such that the primary change between samples is the electronic configuration (VEC).
generation.mechanism: The VEC determines the density of electronic states at the Fermi level which in turn dictates the strength of electron–phonon coupling. An optimal VEC maximizes this coupling to support a higher Tc. Modifying the VEC away from optimum reduces the density of states available for Cooper pairing, thereby lowering Tc—even when disorder levels are similar.
generation.predicted_outcome: High-entropy alloy samples with an optimized (higher) VEC will exhibit a higher Tc compared to those with a lower or non-optimal VEC. This difference in Tc will be observed even though all samples maintain a similar level of structural disorder.
generation.baseline: A reference alloy such as [TaNb]0.31(TiZrHf)0.69 with a well-documented Tc and measured average VEC serves as the baseline for comparison.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys where superconductivity is phonon mediated and follows BCS behavior within the dirty limit. It may not hold if there is a significant deviation in the disorder level, if strong electronic correlations arise, or if non-phononic coupling mechanisms dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence suggests that VEC plays a role (e.g., comparisons between Zr- and U-containing HEAs), the exact quantitative relationship between VEC shifts and Tc variations is uncertain. Additionally, subtle interplay with factors such as spin–orbit coupling may introduce uncertainty in the direct correlation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of HEA samples with identical processing and nearly identical disorder levels but with systematically varied average VEC by substituting one element with another whose valence difference is well defined. For example, prepare alloys based on the [TaNb](TiXHf) system where X is chosen to incrementally change the overall valence electron count. Ensure structural homogeneity using uniform processing protocols.
measurements: Measure Tc via resistivity drop and magnetic susceptibility for superconducting state confirmation.
Use electron diffraction (or related structural characterization) to verify that the degree of disorder remains consistent across all samples.
Characterize the electronic density of states near the Fermi level (e.g., via tunneling spectroscopy or specific heat measurements) to correlate with VEC.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the variations in Tc do not statistically correlate with the induced changes in average VEC—that is, if samples with lower (non-optimal) VEC display Tc values similar to or higher than those with optimized VEC despite comparable disorder—then the hypothesis that VEC governs superconductivity would be falsified.

Robust zero resistance in a superconducting high-entropy alloy at pressures up to 190 GPa

Abstract: SignificanceHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) are made from multiple transition-metal elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. The elements in HEAs arrange themselves randomly on the crystallographic positions of a simple lattice. In addition to their excellent mechanical properties, one HEA has been reported to display superconductivity. In this work, we report that the Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti high-entropy alloy superconductor exhibits extraordinarily robust zero-resistance superconductivity under pressure up to 190.6 GPa. Superconductivity in a uranium containing high entropy alloy

Abstract: High entropy alloys (HEA) are an unusual class of materials where mixtures of elements are stochastically arrayed on a simple crystalline lattice. These systems exhibit remarkable functionality, often along several distinct axes: e.g., the examples [TaNb]1-x(TiZrHf)x are high strength and damage resistant refractory metals that also exhibit superconductivity with large upper critical fields. Here we report the discovery of an f-electron containing HEA, [TaNb]0.31(TiUHf)0.69, which is the first to include an actinide ion. Similar to the Zr-analogue, this material crystallizes in a body-centered cubic lattice with the lattice constant a = 3.41(1) Å and exhibits phonon mediated superconductivity with a transition temperatures Tc ≈ 3.2 K and upper critical fields Hc2 ≈ 6.4 T. These results expand this class of materials to include actinide elements, shows that superconductivity is robust in this sub-group, and opens the path towards leveraging HEAs as functional waste forms for a variety of radioisotopes.

Evidence for isotropic s-wave superconductivity in high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEA) form through the random arrangement of five or more chemical elements on a crystalline lattice. Despite the significant amount of resulting compositional disorder, a subset of HEAs enters a superconducting state below critical temperatures, Tc<10 K. The superconducting properties of the known HEAs seem to suffice a Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) description, but little is known about their superconducting order parameter and the microscopic role of disorder. We report on magnetic susceptibility measurements on films of the superconducting HEA (TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x for characterizing the lower and upper critical fields Hc,1(T) and Hc,2(T), respectively as a function of temperature T. Our resulting analysis of the Ginzburg–Landau coherence length and penetration depth demonstrates that HEAs of this type are single-band isotropic s-wave superconductors in the dirty limit. Despite a significant difference in the elemental composition between the x=0.35 and x=0.71 films, we find that the observed Tc variations cannot be explained by disorder effects.Subject terms: Condensed-
